goal: how to look at the pull requests
preamble: A pull request isn't code, and it isn't a file you'll find by browsing the repository. It's a proposal: someone has work sitting on a branch somewhere and is asking for it to become part of this project. That proposal lives beside the code rather than inside it, which is why looking through the files will never show you one. The row of tabs across the top of a repository is the thing to read — each one is a different view of the same project, and one of them is the view where proposals wait.
generalization: A GitHub repository is not just its files. The tab strip is a list of the parallel things attached to the same project — the code, the problems people have reported, the proposed changes, the automation. When you can't find something by browsing files, the answer is usually that it isn't a file: it's one of those other views, and you switch to it rather than search for it.

steps.intent: You're not looking for a file or a folder — you're looking for the queue of changes people have offered to this project. That queue has its own view, listed alongside the code rather than within it. Switching to it shows every open proposal, who made it, and how long it has been waiting. The number next to it, if there is one, is how many are still open.
hints: You're leaving the files behind. The repository keeps its code in one view and the conversations about changing that code in others — look at the row of views along the top.
The tab strip under the repository name, second from the left after Code, next to Issues.
